paragraphs.text: [Beipu](beipu:where-it-is) is a Hakka township in the south-west of Hsinchu County, in low hill country between the central mountains and the coastal plain, well below the high-mountain oolong gardens. Tea here is a [Hakka trade](hsinchu:hakka): local families grow the leaf, make it and sell it, and on many farms the craft has passed down through generations. The township is counted among the core places for [Oriental Beauty](beipu:known-for), but a label that names Beipu [names a township](beipu:in-hsinchu), not a style.

This [oolong](oolong:definition), a partly oxidised tea that sits between green and red, was made in 1970. Taiwan has a long habit of keeping oolong for years as [lao cha](taiwan-oolong:ageing), old tea. Keepers roast it again at low heat from time to time to drive out the moisture it takes in. No standard says when an oolong becomes old, and those who give a figure put it between ten and thirty years. At fifty-six years, this tea is well beyond either figure.

brewing.text: Ball-rolled Taiwan oolong takes hot water, about 90 to 100°C, a fairly generous amount of leaf and short steeps; the balls open slowly and give many infusions. Roasted Dong Ding takes water from about 95°C to a full boil. Aged oolong takes very hot water, in a pot that holds its heat, clay above all. Oriental Beauty is the exception and takes cooler water, about 80 to 95°C.

notice.text: A smooth, mellow, thick cup with little astringency, often plum or prune, sometimes something like medicinal herbs or ginseng, and an amber to red-brown liquor.
